exercise.html:
Exercise 15.B1 — Medium: Reverify after the input envelope changes

A new sensor calibration gives $z\in[-0.1,0.5]$. Find the exact correction range and decide whether a nominal temperature of 59.7 degrees satisfies the deterministic specification. Exclude the additional residual for this exercise.

Review: ReLU relaxation and branching.

Show hint

The first ReLU is active everywhere on the new interval. Split only at 0.1.

Show worked solution

On $[-0.1,0.1]$, $n=z+0.2$ ranges from 0.1 to 0.3. On $[0.1,0.5]$, $n=0.4-z$ ranges from 0.3 down to $-0.1$. Thus the exact range is $[-0.1,0.3]$. The upper predicted temperature is 60.0 degrees, which satisfies the stated non-strict limit. It has zero certified margin and would fail a requirement of strict separation or any unbudgeted positive implementation error. The old minimum zero cannot be reused after changing the input domain.

exercises.label: Exercise 15.B2 — Hard: Calibrate a whole ten-step forecast

exercise.html:
Exercise 15.B2 — Hard: Calibrate a whole ten-step forecast

For a ten-minute forecast, use the single trajectory score $s=\max_{1\le t\le10}|r_t|$. Require marginal coverage at least 0.99 for the whole residual trajectory. Find the smallest calibration size permitting a finite split-conformal quantile. At that size suppose the chosen quantile is 0.32 degrees. Does nominal temperature 59.35 degrees at every step pass with the same neural upper bound 0.3?

Review: Trajectory-level conformal scores.

Show hint

The order is $\lceil(n+1)0.99\rceil$; it must not exceed $n$. Calibration examples must be entire exchangeable trajectories.

Show worked solution

A finite quantile requires $0.99(n+1)\le n$, equivalently $n\ge99$. At $n=99$, the order is 99, the largest calibration trajectory score. On the event $s\le0.32$, every step has residual magnitude at most 0.32, so each upper temperature is $59.35+0.3+0.32=59.97$ degrees. Under exchangeability of the 99 calibration trajectories and the next trajectory, the event has marginal probability at least 0.99. Calibrating individual time points at 99% separately would not yield the same joint statement; a ten-step union bound would only ensure 90% without an adjusted budget.

exercises.label: Easy 1 — Turn a label claim into a scalar specification

exercise.html:
Easy 1 — Turn a label claim into a scalar specification

On $x\in[0,1]$, logits are $f_1(x)=2x+1$ and $f_2(x)=-x+2$. Write the specification for class 1 to beat class 2, find its worst case, and give a counterexample. If an incomplete verifier returns upper bound $1.4$, does that number alone prove failure?

Review if needed: Primer 0: maxima and bounds; this module's relevant section.

Hint

The scalar violation objective is $f_2-f_1$, not $f_1-f_2$.

Worked solution

Step 1. The violation is $p(x)=f_2(x)-f_1(x)=1-3x$, which is largest at $x=0$, with $p^\star=1$. Thus the desired property fails.

Step 2. The input $x=0$ is an explicit counterexample: the logits are $(1,2)$ and class 2 wins.

Step 3. An upper bound $\bar p=1.4\gt0$ by itself says only that the relaxation did not verify the property. Here failure is established by the actual input and its forward evaluation, not by the positive upper bound.

exercises.label: Easy 2 — One affine interval and one ReLU

exercise.html:
Easy 2 — One affine interval and one ReLU

For $x_1\in[1,2]$, $x_2\in[-1,1]$, find the exact interval for $z=2x_1-3x_2+1$ and its ReLU output. Give input corners attaining the two endpoints.

Review if needed: Primer 0: maxima and bounds; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Positive coefficients maximize at the upper input endpoint; negative coefficients maximize at the lower endpoint.

Worked solution

Step 1. The minimum is $2(1)-3(1)+1=0$, attained at $(1,1)$. The maximum is $2(2)-3(-1)+1=8$, attained at $(2,-1)$. Hence $z\in[0,8]$.

Step 2. ReLU is monotone, so its output interval is $[\operatorname{ReLU}(0),\operatorname{ReLU}(8)]=[0,8]$. This neuron is stable active, including its zero boundary.

Step 3. In centre-radius form the input centre is $(1.5,0)$ and radius $(0.5,1)$; the pre-activation centre is $4$ and radius $2(0.5)+3(1)=4$, giving the same result.

exercises.label: Easy 3 — An unstable ReLU triangle

exercise.html:
Easy 3 — An unstable ReLU triangle

On $z\in[-2,3]$ write the chord upper bound and choose lower line $h_L(z)=0.4z$. Check both inequalities at $z=-1$ and $z=1$. Why is a negative lower-line value allowed?

Review if needed: Primer B: convex relaxations; this module's relevant section.

Hint

The chord joins $(-2,0)$ to $(3,3)$. A lower bound need not be an attainable activation value.

Worked solution

Step 1. The chord is $h_U(z)=\frac35(z+2)$. At $z=-1$, $h_L=-0.4\le0=\operatorname{ReLU}(-1)\le0.6=h_U$.

Step 2. At $z=1$, $h_L=0.4\le1\le1.8=h_U$. More generally, $0\le0.4\le1$ makes $0.4z$ a valid ReLU lower line across the entire interval.

Step 3. A relaxation encloses the true graph and may include artificial points. A negative lower value is conservative, while a lower value above the actual ReLU would be unsound.

exercises.label: Easy 4 — Choose the conformal order statistic

exercise.html:
Easy 4 — Choose the conformal order statistic

Nine calibration scores sorted increasingly are $0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9$. At miscoverage level $\alpha=0.2$, compute the split-conformal index and threshold. For absolute-error scores and prediction $\hat y=2$, write the prediction interval.

Review if needed: Primer C: binomial tails and exchangeability; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Use $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, with $n+1$, not $n$.

Worked solution

Step 1. $k=\lceil10(0.8)\rceil=8$, so the threshold is the eighth calibration score, $\hat q=0.8$.

Step 2. The set $|y-2|\le0.8$ is the interval $[1.2,2.8]$. The endpoints are included because the conformal set uses $\le$.

Step 3. With a score fixed before calibration and exchangeable calibration/test examples, the marginal coverage is at least $0.8$. The theorem averages over calibration and test randomness; it is not a guarantee at each individual input.

exercise.html:
Medium 1 — Interval independence can invent an impossible output

For $x\in[-1,1]$, let $a_1=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)$, $a_2=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)$, $f=a_1-a_2$. Compute the IBP output interval and the exact output set. What information did IBP discard?

Review if needed: Primer A: matrix arithmetic; this module's relevant section.

Hint

The two activation intervals are identical, but their values cannot be chosen independently.

Worked solution

Step 1. Each hidden interval is $[0,1]$. Treating them as independent gives $f\in[0-1,1-0]=[-1,1]$.

Step 2. The exact network always has $a_1=a_2$, so $f(x)=0$ and the exact output set is $\{0\}$.

Step 3. IBP kept coordinate ranges and forgot equality between the coordinates. It remains sound because $\{0\}\subset[-1,1]$. A relaxation preserving this equality, or algebraic cancellation before bounding, recovers the tighter result.

exercise.html:
Medium 2 — Select a CROWN line by the output sign

Let $f(z)=1-2\operatorname{ReLU}(z)$ on $[-1,2]$, with upper chord $h_U(z)=\frac23(z+1)$ and lower line $h_L=0$. Which line gives an upper bound on $f$, and which a lower bound? Show at $z=-1/2$ why using $1-2h_U$ as an upper bound fails.

Review if needed: Primer 0: signed arithmetic and inequalities; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Multiplying an activation inequality by $-2$ reverses its direction.

Worked solution

Step 1. From $h_L\le\operatorname{ReLU}(z)\le h_U$ we get $1-2h_U\le f(z)\le1-2h_L=1$. Thus the lower activation line supplies the upper output bound.

Step 2. The lower output line is $1-\frac43(z+1)$, whose minimum on the interval is $-3$ at $z=2$. The exact function ranges from $-3$ to $1$, so both final scalar bounds are tight here.

Step 3. At $z=-1/2$, the actual output is $1$, while $1-2h_U=1-2(1/3)=1/3$. It cannot be an upper bound on a value equal to $1$; it is a valid lower bound.

exercises.label: Medium 3 — A smoothing radius and its confidence statement

exercise.html:
Medium 3 — A smoothing radius and its confidence statement

An independent Monte-Carlo confidence procedure returns $\underline p_A=\Phi(2)\approx0.977249868$ at confidence $99.9\%$, with Gaussian noise scale $\sigma=0.5$. Compute the certified Euclidean radius and a sufficient infinity-norm radius in dimension $100$. What happens if the lower bound is instead $0.5$?

Review if needed: Primer C: Gaussian quantiles; this module's relevant section.

Hint

The single-probability rule is $R=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)$.

Worked solution

Step 1. Because $\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(2))=2$, the Euclidean radius is $R=0.5(2)=1$. On the confidence event, the ideal smoothed classifier keeps label $A$ for all perturbations with Euclidean norm strictly below $1$.

Step 2. $\|\delta\|_2\le\sqrt{100}\|\delta\|_\infty=10\|\delta\|_\infty$, so a sufficient strict infinity-norm radius is $0.1$.

Step 3. The confidence is over the probability-estimation samples, and the certified object is the smoothed classifier. If $\underline p_A=0.5$, the rule produces zero radius and CERTIFY abstains; it does not supply a positive-radius certificate.

exercises.label: Medium 4 — Validation needs a sampling margin

exercise.html:
Medium 4 — Validation needs a sampling margin

A fixed controller is evaluated on fresh i.i.d. trials with a success indicator in $[0,1]$. At one-sided confidence $99\%$ and tolerance $t=0.1$, compute the sufficient Hoeffding sample size. If the observed success fraction is $0.98$, what population success lower bound follows? Can this tolerance certify target success $0.95$?

Review if needed: Primer C: confidence events and union bounds; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Use $M\ge\ln(1/\alpha)/(2t^2)$ and subtract $t$ from the observed fraction.

Worked solution

Step 1. Here $\alpha=0.01$, so $M\ge\ln100/0.02\approx230.25851$. The integer sample count is at least $231$.

Step 2. With probability at least $0.99$, the population success probability is at least $\hat\phi-t=0.98-0.1=0.88$. The observed fraction itself is not the population guarantee.

Step 3. To certify population success $0.95$ with this tolerance would require $\hat\phi\ge1.05$, which is impossible. Reduce $t$ and increase the sample size; keep validation independent of controller selection or account for selection explicitly.

exercises.label: Hard 1 — The same affine bound over different input balls

exercise.html:
Hard 1 — The same affine bound over different input balls

A backward relaxation yields the exact affine expression $g(x)=3x_1-4x_2+2$. Around $x_0=(1,2)$ with radius $\varepsilon=0.2$, compute its ranges for Euclidean and infinity-norm input balls, and give perturbations attaining the lower endpoints. Explain why the radii cannot be exchanged unchanged.

Review if needed: Primer A: norm comparisons and dual norms; this module's relevant section.

Hint

The dual norms of the coefficient row $(3,-4)$ are $5$ for an $\ell_2$ ball and $7$ for an $\ell_\infty$ ball.

Worked solution

Step 1. The centre value is $3-8+2=-3$. On the Euclidean ball, the deviation is bounded by $0.2\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}=1$, so the exact range is $[-4,-2]$. The lower endpoint is attained by $\delta=-0.2(3,-4)/5=(-0.12,0.16)$.

Step 2. On the infinity-norm ball, the deviation is $0.2(|3|+|-4|)=1.4$, giving $[-4.4,-1.6]$. The minimizing perturbation is $\delta=(-0.2,0.2)$, choosing the sign against each coefficient.

Step 3. The infinity-norm ball with the same numerical radius contains vectors with larger Euclidean norm. The correct dual norm is part of the specification; reusing the Euclidean bound unchanged on that larger set would miss attainable values.

exercises.label: Hard 2 — A trajectory budget and finite calibration resolution

exercise.html:
Hard 2 — A trajectory budget and finite calibration resolution

For four future times you want total miscoverage at most $0.1$. Allocate equal per-time budgets and compute the conformal order index for $n=39$ and for $n=19$ calibration trajectories. Would using $90\%$ marginal coverage at every time alone imply $90\%$ joint coverage?

Review if needed: Primer C: confidence events and union bounds; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Use a union bound, then compare $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ with $n$.

Worked solution

Step 1. Choose per-time miscoverage $\alpha=0.1/4=0.025$. Then the union bound gives joint coverage at least $1-4(0.025)=0.9$ without requiring independence between times.

Step 2. For $n=39$, $k=\lceil40(0.975)\rceil=39$, so the threshold is the largest observed score. For $n=19$, $k=\lceil20(0.975)\rceil=20\gt19$, so the valid threshold is $+\infty$; the data cannot supply a finite threshold at this nominal resolution.

Step 3. Four marginal $90\%$ statements give only the union-bound lower bound $1-4(0.1)=0.6$. Even independent $90\%$ coverage events would have joint probability $0.9^4=0.6561$, not $0.9$. A horizon guarantee needs its own budget and the exchangeability assumptions.

exercise.html:
Hard 3 — Compare an exact scenario tail with an explicit bound

A scenario program meets the theorem assumptions with $d=3$, target violation $\varepsilon=0.1$ and design failure probability $\beta=0.05$. Compute the explicit sufficient integer count from $N\ge\frac2\varepsilon(\ln(1/\beta)+d)$. Check the exact binomial tail at $N=60$ and $61$. State what probability is bounded.

Review if needed: Primer C: binomial tails and exchangeability; this module's relevant section.

Hint

For $d=3$, sum the binomial probabilities for $i=0,1,2$. The outer randomness is the design sample.

Worked solution

Step 1. The explicit rule gives $N\ge20(\ln20+3)\approx119.91465$, so $N=120$ suffices.

exercises.label: Hard 4 — Conditioning on planner feasibility changes the bound

exercise.html:
Hard 4 — Conditioning on planner feasibility changes the bound

A conformal planning argument proves $\mathbb P(\text{feasible and unsafe})\le0.04$, while $\mathbb P(\text{feasible})=0.5$. What upper bound follows on failure conditional on feasibility? Does the argument prove unconditional safety at least $0.96$ if behavior on infeasible runs is unspecified?

Review if needed: Primer C: conditional probability; this module's relevant section.

Hint

Use the definition of conditional probability; the event inclusion controls only one part of all runs.

Worked solution

Step 1. $\mathbb P(\text{unsafe}\mid\text{feasible})=\mathbb P(\text{unsafe and feasible})/0.5\le0.04/0.5=0.08$. Thus the conditional safety lower bound from these facts is $0.92$.

Step 2. Infeasible runs have probability $0.5$ and may all be unsafe. The given facts alone therefore permit unconditional unsafe probability as high as $0.5+0.04=0.54$, yielding only the lower bound $0.46$ on safety.

Step 3. To obtain the intended unconditional safety statement, prove almost-sure feasibility or add a certified safe fallback for infeasible cases. Simply discarding infeasible runs changes the probability space and does not preserve the original $0.96$ claim.

exercise.html:
Exercise 15.1 — Derive the IBP affine rule and exhibit its joint looseness

(a) Let $a\in[\underline a,\overline a]$ and $z=Wa+b$. Derive the interval $[\underline z,\overline z]$ produced by IBP and show that each coordinate bound is attained. (b) For $W=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$, $b=0$ and $a\in[-1,1]^2$, describe the true image $\{Wa\}$ and find a point of the IBP box that is not in it.

Show answer

(a) Write $a=\mu+\delta$ with $\mu=\tfrac12(\overline a+\underline a)$, $|\delta_j|\le r_j=\tfrac12(\overline a_j-\underline a_j)$. Then $z_i=W_{i,:}\mu+b_i+W_{i,:}\delta$ and $|W_{i,:}\delta|\le\sum_j|W_{ij}||\delta_j|\le\sum_j|W_{ij}|r_j=(|W|r)_i$ (triangle inequality, then $|\delta_j|\le r_j$). So $\underline z=W\mu+b-|W|r$, $\overline z=W\mu+b+|W|r$. Choosing $\delta_j=r_j\,\mathrm{sign}(W_{ij})$ makes every term $|W_{ij}|r_j$ and this $\delta$ is feasible, so $\overline z_i$ is attained; $\delta_j=-r_j\,\mathrm{sign}(W_{ij})$ attains $\underline z_i$.

(b) $\mu=0$, $r=(1,1)$, $|W|r=(2,2)$: IBP gives $z\in[-2,2]^2$. The true image is the set of $(a_1+a_2,\,a_1-a_2)$ with $|a_i|\le1$, a square rotated by $45^\circ$ with vertices $(\pm2,0)$ and $(0,\pm2)$ (equivalently $|z_1|+|z_2|\le 2$). The IBP corner $(2,2)$ would need $a_1+a_2=2$ and $a_1-a_2=2$, i.e. $a_1=2$, which is infeasible. The box has area 16, the image has area 8: IBP doubles the area in a single layer, and the next layer may combine $z_1=2$ with $z_2=2$ as if both were reachable at once.

exercise.html:
Exercise 15.2 — CROWN bounds for the walkthrough network at other radii

Repeat the walkthrough for the same network and $x_0=(1,1)$ with (a) $\varepsilon=0.5$ and (b) $\varepsilon=1.5$: give the pre-activation bounds, the neuron statuses, the IBP interval, the adaptive-CROWN interval, the α-CROWN lower bound and the exact range. Check with Panel A.

Show answer

(a) $\varepsilon=0.5$: $r=|W|(0.5,0.5)^{\top}=(1,1.5)$, so $z_1\in[2,4]$, $z_2\in[0.5,3.5]$: both neurons stable active. IBP: $a_1\in[2,4]$, $a_2\in[0.5,3.5]$, $f\in[-8+1,\,-4+7]=[-7,3]$. CROWN needs no relaxation: $f=-2z_1+2z_2=-4x_1+2x_2$ exactly, $\Omega=(-4,2)$, $\Omega x_0=-2$, $\|\Omega\|_1=6$, so $f\in[-2-3,\,-2+3]=[-5,1]$, which is also the exact range (attained at $(1.5,0.5)$ and $(0.5,1.5)$). Lesson: IBP is loose even without any unstable neuron, purely through the joint-box effect of Exercise 15.1; CROWN is exact for an affine function.

(b) $\varepsilon=1.5$: $r=(3,4.5)$, $z_1\in[0,6]$ (stable active, $l_1=0$), $z_2\in[-2.5,6.5]$ (unstable). IBP: $a_1\in[0,6]$, $a_2\in[0,6.5]$, $f\in[-12,13]$. Adaptive CROWN: $u_2=6.5\ge|l_2|$ so $\alpha=1$; lower line $z_2$, upper chord $\tfrac{6.5}{9}(z_2+2.5)$. Lower bound: $f\ge-2z_1+2\alpha z_2$ with $\Omega=(-2-2\alpha,\,-2+4\alpha)$, $c=-2+2\alpha$, giving $\gamma^L(\alpha)=-6+4\alpha-1.5\,(2+2\alpha+|4\alpha-2|)=-9+\alpha-1.5|4\alpha-2|$: $\gamma^L(1)=-11$ (CROWN), $\gamma^L(0)=-12$ (= IBP), maximum $\gamma^L(\tfrac12)=-8.5$ (α-CROWN). Upper bound: $\Lambda=(-\tfrac{31}{9},\tfrac89)$, $c_U=\tfrac{55}{18}$, $\Lambda x_0+c_U=\tfrac12$, $\gamma^U=\tfrac12+1.5\cdot\tfrac{39}{9}=7$. Exact: on $\{z_2\ge0\}$, $f=-4x_1+2x_2$ with minimum $-8.5$ at the kink point $(2.5,0.75)$ and maximum $7$ at $(-0.5,2.5)$; on $\{z_2\le0\}$, $f=-2x_1-2x_2-2\ge-8.5$. exercise.html:
Exercise 15.3 — Prove the split-conformal coverage bound

Let $s_1,\dots,s_n,s_{n+1}$ be exchangeable, almost surely distinct scores ($s_{n+1}$ is the test score) and $\hat q=s_{(k)}$ with $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\le n$. (a) Prove $\mathbb P(s_{n+1}\le\hat q)=k/(n+1)$. (b) Deduce $1-\alpha\le\mathbb P(s_{n+1}\le\hat q)\lt1-\alpha+\tfrac1{n+1}$. (c) For $n=9$, $\alpha=0.1$, what is $\hat q$ and what is the exact coverage? (d) Why does the lower bound survive ties while the upper bound may not?

Show answer

(a) Let $\rho$ be the rank of $s_{n+1}$ among the $n+1$ scores. Exchangeability means the joint law is invariant under permutations, so $\mathbb P(\rho=r)$ is the same for every $r\in\{1,\dots,n+1\}$, hence $1/(n+1)$. The event $s_{n+1}\le s_{(k)}$ (the $k$-th smallest of the other $n$ scores) means that at most $k-1$ of the others are smaller than $s_{n+1}$, i.e. $\rho\le k$. Therefore $\mathbb P(s_{n+1}\le\hat q)=\mathbb P(\rho\le k)=k/(n+1)$.

(b) By definition of the ceiling, $(n+1)(1-\alpha)\le k\lt(n+1)(1-\alpha)+1$; divide by $n+1$.

(c) $k=\lceil 10\cdot0.9\rceil=9$: $\hat q$ is the largest calibration score and the coverage is exactly $9/10=0.9$ (the prediction set is as tight as the guarantee allows, but only because $(n+1)(1-\alpha)$ is an integer; for $n=10$ one gets $k=\lceil9.9\rceil=10$ and coverage $10/11\approx0.909$).

(d) With ties, attach an independent uniform tie-breaker $U_i$ to every score and order the pairs $(s_i,U_i)$ lexicographically. The pairs are exchangeable and almost surely distinct, so by (a) the rank $\rho$ of the test pair satisfies $\mathbb P(\rho\le k)=k/(n+1)$. If $\rho\le k$, at most $k-1$ calibration pairs precede the test pair, so at most $k-1$ calibration scores are strictly smaller than $s_{n+1}$ and $s_{n+1}\le s_{(k)}=\hat q$. Hence $\mathbb P(s_{n+1}\le\hat q)\ge k/(n+1)$: the lower bound is safe. The converse fails: a test score tied with $s_{(k)}$ is covered even when its tie-breaker ranks it after position $k$, and the probability can exceed $k/(n+1)$ by the mass of ties at $s_{(k)}$; the upper bound $1-\alpha+\tfrac1{n+1}$ therefore requires almost surely distinct joint scores (for example, independent and identically distributed continuous scores) or independent randomised tie-breaking for both calibration and test/prediction membership. In the extreme case of a constant score, $\mathcal C$ always contains everything and coverage is 1.

exercise.html:
Exercise 15.4 — Certified radii of a smoothed classifier

A smoothed classifier uses $\sigma=0.5$. (a) CERTIFY returns the lower confidence bound $\underline{p_A}=0.95$; what radius does it certify? (b) Suppose one additionally knew $\overline{p_B}=0.03$; what radius does Theorem 1 give? (c) What is the largest radius CERTIFY can ever return with $n=10^4$ samples and $\alpha=0.001$, and why? Use $\Phi^{-1}(0.95)=1.645$, $\Phi^{-1}(0.97)=1.881$, $\Phi^{-1}(0.001^{1/10^4})=\Phi^{-1}(0.99931)=3.20$.

Show answer

(a) CERTIFY sets $\overline{p_B}=1-\underline{p_A}=0.05$, so $R=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}(\Phi^{-1}(0.95)-\Phi^{-1}(0.05))=\tfrac\sigma2\cdot2\cdot1.645=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(0.95)=0.5\cdot1.645=0.82$. The statement “$g$ is constant on the $\ell_2$ ball of radius 0.82” holds with probability at least $0.999$ over the Monte-Carlo draw.

(b) $R=\tfrac{0.5}{2}\big(\Phi^{-1}(0.95)-\Phi^{-1}(0.03)\big)=0.25\,(1.645+1.881)=0.88$: knowing that the runner-up is weak buys a little, which is why the multiclass bound is stated with both numbers, but CERTIFY does not estimate $\overline{p_B}$ separately because it would cost a second confidence bound.

(c) Even if all $n$ samples return $\hat c_A$, the one-sided Clopper–Pearson bound is $\underline{p_A}=\alpha^{1/n}=0.001^{10^{-4}}\approx0.99931$, so $R_{\max}=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(0.99931)=0.5\cdot3.20=1.60$. The radius saturates because $1-\alpha^{1/n}\approx\ln(1/\alpha)/n$ and $\Phi^{-1}(1-p)$ grows only like $\sqrt{2\ln(1/p)}$: going from $n=10^4$ to $10^5$ moves the cap from $3.20\sigma$ to $3.81\sigma$, only $0.6\sigma$ for ten times the compute. This is the Monte-Carlo price that a deterministic Lipschitz certificate does not pay.

Use $\Phi^{-1}(0.95)=1.645$, $\Phi^{-1}(0.97)=1.881$, $\Phi^{-1}(0.001^{1/10^4})=\Phi^{-1}(0.99931)=3.20$.

(a) CERTIFY sets $\overline{p_B}=1-\underline{p_A}=0.05$, so $R=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}(\Phi^{-1}(0.95)-\Phi^{-1}(0.05))=\tfrac\sigma2\cdot2\cdot1.645=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(0.95)=0.5\cdot1.645=0.82$. The statement “$g$ is constant on the $\ell_2$ ball of radius 0.82” holds with probability at least $0.999$ over the Monte-Carlo draw.

(b) $R=\tfrac{0.5}{2}\big(\Phi^{-1}(0.95)-\Phi^{-1}(0.03)\big)=0.25\,(1.645+1.881)=0.88$: knowing that the runner-up is weak buys a little, which is why the multiclass bound is stated with both numbers, but CERTIFY does not estimate $\overline{p_B}$ separately because it would cost a second confidence bound.

(c) Even if all $n$ samples return $\hat c_A$, the one-sided Clopper–Pearson bound is $\underline{p_A}=\alpha^{1/n}=0.001^{10^{-4}}\approx0.99931$, so $R_{\max}=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(0.99931)=0.5\cdot3.20=1.60$. exercise.html:
Exercise 15.5 — Scenario sample sizes: explicit, exact and old

A robust design problem has $d=10$ decision variables; we want violation at most $\varepsilon=0.05$ with confidence $1-\beta=1-10^{-6}$. (a) Compute the explicit sample size $N\ge\tfrac2\varepsilon(\ln\tfrac1\beta+d)$. (b) Explain in two lines where the Chernoff argument uses $d\le N\varepsilon$. (c) The exact binomial-tail solution is $N=643$ and the 2006 bound $\binom Nd(1-\varepsilon)^{N-d}\le\beta$ needs $N=1396$; comment on the three numbers. (d) In von Rohr et al. (2021) the decision variables of the initial LMI (their eq. 4) are the entries of the $d_x\times d_x$ matrices $Y$ (the inverse Lyapunov matrix) and $Z$ (a slack) and of the $d_u\times d_x$ matrix $KY$ (called $L$ in the paper), counted as $n_k=2d_x^2+d_xd_u$; how many scenarios does the explicit bound require for $d_x=4$, $d_u=1$ with $\varepsilon=0.05$, $\beta=10^{-3}$?

Show answer

(a) $\ln(10^6)=13.816$, so $N\ge\tfrac{2}{0.05}(13.816+10)=40\cdot23.816=952.6$: take $N=953$.

(b) The Chernoff lower-tail bound $\mathbb P(X\le(1-t)\mu)\le e^{-t^2\mu/2}$ needs $t\in[0,1]$; writing $d=(1-t)\mu$ gives $t=1-d/\mu$, which lies in $[0,1]$ exactly when $d\le\mu=N\varepsilon$. With $N\varepsilon=2\ln\tfrac1\beta+2d\ge d$ this is automatic.

(c) $643\lt953\lt1396$. The exact value is smallest because Theorem 2.4 is tight for fully supported problems; the explicit bound throws away the $d^2$ slack in the Chernoff step and the difference between $\mathbb P(X\le d-1)$ and $\mathbb P(X\le d)$, costing about 50% more samples; the 2006 bound is looser still because $\binom Nd(1-\varepsilon)^{N-d}$ counts each choice of $d$ support constraints separately instead of the binomial event. All three are distribution-free: nothing about the plant or the uncertainty entered.

(d) $n_k=2\cdot16+4=36$, $\ln(10^3)=6.908$: $N\ge40\,(6.908+36)=1716.3$, so $N=1717$ sampled models, each adding one LMI to the common-Lyapunov scenario program (solving the exact binomial condition instead would give $N=1138$). Two remarks. The paper truncates the posterior for a different reason, but the untruncated posterior would matter for Assumption 1 (every sampled program feasible). The untruncated matrix-normal posterior is nondegenerate (Primer C), so its support is the whole parameter space, and for every gain $K$ the unstable systems $\{\rho(A+BK)\gt1\}$ form a non-empty open set of positive probability. That fixed-gain fact alone does not break Assumption 1, because the scenario program chooses $K$ after seeing the samples; what breaks it is a sample containing models with no common stabilising gain, and full support gives such samples positive probability. For $d_x=d_u=1$, $|A+BK|\lt1$ means $K\in\big((-1-A)/B,\,(1-A)/B\big)$ for $B\gt0$: models close to $(A,B)=(3,1)$ need $K$ near $(-4,-2)$ and models close to $(-3,1)$ need $K$ near $(2,4)$, so a sample with one model in each of two small neighbourhoods (positive probability once $M\ge2$) makes the common-Lyapunov LMI infeasible; for the paper’s matrix-valued program such an incompatible pair has to be exhibited in the same way. Unbounded support alone would not force this: if $A=0$ almost surely, $K=0$ stabilises every $B$. Nor does truncation alone restore it; Assumption 1 must still hold on the truncated support, which the paper notes may contain unstabilisable systems. And the improvement steps after the initial LMI are not scenario programs, so the final gain is validated a posteriori with Hoeffding instead.

exercise.html:
Exercise 15.6 — Why the smoothing certificate is probabilistic and the Lipschitz certificate is not

A colleague claims that “71% certified accuracy at $\ell_2$ radius 0.5 on ImageNet” (denoised smoothing) is a strictly stronger result than “41% certified accuracy at radius 0.14” (LipNeXt). List every way in which the two statements differ in kind, not just in number, and state precisely what each certifies.

Show answer

Object certified. The Lipschitz certificate is about the trained network $f$ itself: since $\|f(x)-f(x')\|\le L\|x-x'\|$ and the margin at $x$ is $M$, every $x'$ with $\|x'-x\|\lt M/(\sqrt2L)$ has the same argmax. The smoothing certificate is about $g(x)=\arg\max_c\mathbb P(f(x+\varepsilon)=c)$, a different classifier that is never evaluated exactly.

Nature of the statement. The Lipschitz statement is a theorem, true for all perturbations in the ball with probability one. The smoothing statement is a confidence statement: CERTIFY’s radius is correct with probability $\ge1-\alpha$ over its own $10^4$–$10^5$ random forward passes, and Theorem 1 itself needs the true $p_A$, which is only bounded statistically. The guarantee is per input: for each fixed test input, $\mathbb P(\text{CERTIFY returns a wrong certificate})\le\alpha$. Over $M$ test inputs the expected number of wrong certificates is therefore at most $M\alpha$, but this bounds neither the realised number nor the error probability given that a certificate was returned, $\mathbb P(\text{wrong}\mid\text{returned})=\mathbb P(\text{returns a wrong certificate})/\mathbb P(\text{returned})$, which can exceed $\alpha$.

Prediction. $g$ itself is deterministic (once ties are broken by a fixed rule) but cannot be computed exactly, so it is deployed as the Monte-Carlo procedure PREDICT. PREDICT is random and can abstain; except with probability at most $\alpha$ it returns $g(x)$ or abstains (Cohen et al., Proposition 1), and it costs $n$ forward passes ($n=100$ in the paper’s experiments, against $10^5$ for CERTIFY). $f$ is deterministic and costs one.

Threat model and dimension. Gaussian smoothing certifies $\ell_2$ balls and its $\ell_\infty$ radius shrinks with the dimension; a Lipschitz bound in the $\ell_2$ norm converts to $\ell_\infty$ through norm equivalence ($\|v\|_2\le\sqrt d\,\|v\|_\infty$) at the same dimension-dependent cost, whereas the bound-propagation and SDP verifiers of Sections 2–3 handle $\ell_\infty$ boxes directly.

What each number means. 71% = fraction of test images for which CERTIFY returned the correct class and a radius $\ge0.5$ (each certificate holding with probability $1-\alpha$ over CERTIFY’s sampling, in the protocol of Cohen et al. that Carlini et al. follow, and using extra pretraining data); 41% = fraction of test images for which the deterministic margin-over-Lipschitz radius is $\ge36/255$. The first is larger and at a larger radius; it is also weaker in kind, and neither says anything about perturbations outside the $\ell_2$ threat model.

The guarantee is per input: for each fixed test input, $\mathbb P(\text{CERTIFY returns a wrong certificate})\le\alpha$. Over $M$ test inputs the expected number of wrong certificates is therefore at most $M\alpha$, but this bounds neither the realised number nor the error probability given that a certificate was returned, $\mathbb P(\text{wrong}\mid\text{returned})=\mathbb P(\text{returns a wrong certificate})/\mathbb P(\text{returned})$, which can exceed $\alpha$.

Prediction. $g$ itself is deterministic (once ties are broken by a fixed rule) but cannot be computed exactly, so it is deployed as the Monte-Carlo procedure PREDICT. PREDICT is random and can abstain; except with probability at most $\alpha$ it returns $g(x)$ or abstains (Cohen et al., Proposition 1), and it costs $n$ forward passes ($n=100$ in the paper’s experiments, against $10^5$ for CERTIFY). $f$ is deterministic and costs one.

Threat model and dimension. Gaussian smoothing certifies $\ell_2$ balls and its $\ell_\infty$ radius shrinks with the dimension; a Lipschitz bound in the $\ell_2$ norm converts to $\ell_\infty$ through norm equivalence ($\|v\|_2\le\sqrt d\,\|v\|_\infty$) at the same dimension-dependent cost, whereas the bound-propagation and SDP verifiers of Sections 2–3 handle $\ell_\infty$ boxes directly.

What each number means. 71% = fraction of test images for which CERTIFY returned the correct class and a radius $\ge0.5$ (each certificate holding with probability $1-\alpha$ over CERTIFY’s sampling, in the protocol of Cohen et al. that Carlini et al. follow, and using extra pretraining data); 41% = fraction of test images for which the deterministic margin-over-Lipschitz radius is $\ge36/255$. The first is larger and at a larger radius; it is also weaker in kind, and neither says anything about perturbations outside the $\ell_2$ threat model.
